Nephrotic Syndrome

Overview

Normally, protein molecules shouldn’t be lost in urine in concentrations higher than 150 mg per day

If the urine protein excretion exceeds 150 mg per day then this is called proteinuria and it is caused by many diseases including UTI, nephrotic syndrome, CKD…

When the urine protein become > 3.5 g per day then it is called nephrotic range proteinuria and it is caused by nephrotic syndrome

Cause

In nephrotic syndrome the kidney glomerulus would have some kind of problem that make it pass protein molecules into the urine, the problem exactly in the podocyte (NephrOtic = POdocyte)

Pathophysiology

Due to the albumin lost in urine, liver tries to compensate by increasing albumin synthesis but it fails to reach the normal albumin levels

As a result of the protein lost in urine, the oncotic pressure decreases which stimulate the hepatic lipoprotein synthesis which lead to hypercholesterolemia and hypertriglyceridemia

Lipid become entrapped in casts and enclosed by the plasma membrane of a degenerative renal tubular cells which lead to oval fat body in urine

Presentation

Frothy urine

Edema

Swelling around the eye (periorbital edema)

Ascites

Dyspnea due to pleural effusion or due to diaphragmatic compression with ascites

Hypertension

Hyperlipidemia (serum cholesterol > 300)

Proteinuria (3.5 g/day)

Hypoalbuminemia

Anemia because transferrin is also lost in urine

Increase risk of infection

Increased risk of thrombosis

Diagnosis

Best initial test is urinalysis which detect protein lost in urine, and any urinary casts

24 hour urine protein test

Normal protein excretion < 150 mg/day

Nephrotic range > 3.5 g/day

Urine protein to creatinine ratio

Easier to obtain than 24 hours urine collection

Comprehensive metabolic panel looking for hypoalbuminemia (normal albumin= 3.5-5 g/dl)

Renal function test: blood urea nitrogen and creatinine

Serum electrolytes and lipid profile looking for any changes

Confirmatory test is renal biopsy looking for the exact pathology

Treatment

Curative treatment

Treat the cause usually with immunosuppressive therapy

Supportive treatment

Strict blood pressure control < 130/80 mmHg using ACEs or ARBs

Hyperlipidemia treated with statins

Edema treated with sodium restriction and diuretics

Thrombophilia treated with anticoagulation

Infections treated with antibiotics

Complications

Thrombosis

Thrombosis typically seen in > 10g of proteinuria

Coagulation and anti coagulation factors are lost into the urine including anti thrombin III factor

Thrombosis

Liver tries to compensate for that by making more pro coagulation factors which make the problem worse

Volume depletion from diuretic therapy and reduced oncotic pressure lead to hemoconcentration and increased PLT aggregation which lead to thrombus formation and thrombosis

Infection

Immunoglobulins lost in urine

Patient become more susceptible to infections mostly with staphylococci and streptococci bacteria

Acute renal failure Due to hypovolemia (fluid shifted from intravascular into tissues = edema)

Pulmonary edema

Growth retardation

Etiology

Primary glomerular diseases include immune mediated injury to the podocytes

  • Minimal change disease
  • Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
  • Membranous nephropathy
  • Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis

Secondary glomerular diseases includes systemic diseases that also affect the glomerulus

  • Amyloidosis
  • Diabetic nephropathy
  • Systemic lupus erythematosus (lupus nephritis)
